\subsection{Evaluation, Statistics and Report Assembly (Member 3)}\label{ch6:sec:m3}
Member 3's module is the \path{eval/} package and the \path{fixtures/od-fixture} project: it
turns Member 2's raw run counts into a Wilson interval and a typed outcome, assembles and
schema-validates the diagnosis report, and owns the seeded fixture every real result in this
report is measured against. It is 913 lines of Python across six files, with 1{,}231 lines of
tests (\texttt{wc -l}, 11 October 2026).

\subsubsection{Wilson interval, not Wald}
Every reproduction rate in this report is a Wilson score interval, not the textbook Wald
interval, because Brown, Cai and DasGupta show Wald's coverage is ``chaotic'' at the sample
sizes this project actually uses --- D3 in the claims ledger. \texttt{wilson\_interval} is
tested against \texttt{statsmodels}'s own implementation (\path{eval/tests/test\_stats.py}) so
the estimator itself does not drift from the literature it is supposed to match. The threshold
that turns an interval into \texttt{VERIFIED} (lower bound $\geq 0.70$) is a separate,
explicitly \textbf{project-policy} decision --- the certificate contract states this distinction
on purpose, because panels respect ``that is our acceptance policy, frozen on [date]'' and
punish blurring it with a published finding.

\subsubsection{The outcome decision table}
\texttt{decide()} implements the table in Figure~\ref{ch5:fig:outcome}, evaluated top to bottom,
first match wins: source integrity, then whether the victim fails alone, then whether the
sequence reproduces at all (split further into clean/infrastructure-failure/signature-mismatch
sub-cases added by ADR-008), then whether a resource edge exists, then the Wilson threshold.
Ranking alone can never produce \texttt{VERIFIED} --- a concrete resource edge is always
required alongside the statistics, which is the one rule the schema itself does not enforce (it
is enforced in code, by \texttt{decide()} requiring \texttt{resource\_edge\_exists} before
reaching the threshold check at all).

\subsubsection{Report assembly}
\texttt{assemble\_report} combines a \texttt{DiagnosisRuns} (Member 2), resource fields (Member
1, via \texttt{report\_fields}/\texttt{combine\_fields}) and \texttt{decide()}'s verdict into one
dict, then \texttt{validate\_report} checks it against the schema before \texttt{runner/cli.py}
saves it --- an invalid report is never written. Three of \texttt{DiagnosisRuns}'s four statuses
are handled (\texttt{POLLUTER\_FOUND}, \texttt{VICTIM\_FAILS\_ALONE}, \texttt{NOT\_REPRODUCED});
\texttt{NO\_SINGLE\_POLLUTER} is deliberately not, since the schema has no
\texttt{unresolved\_reason} for it yet (\texttt{UnhandledStatus}, exit code 3 from Member 2's
CLI) --- a real, open question, not an oversight.

\subsubsection{The fixture suite}
\path{fixtures/od-fixture} has seven real cases, their expected outcomes written to
\path{ground_truth.json} before any run against them: F1--F4 are order-dependent (single
static-field write, a system property read one call below the test, two polluters both
required, and a case the discovered order can never reproduce without a shuffle); N1--N3 are
negative controls (fails alone deterministically, fails alone intermittently, and an
externally-caused failure FlakeTrace never observes). Every one matches its pre-registered
ground truth exactly as of this report (Table~\ref{ch8:tab:cases}).

\subsubsection{Testing}
268 tests pass across the whole project; this module's own suite is 7 files under
\path{eval/tests/}, including a scriptable \texttt{FakeOrderRunner} that lives only there and is
never imported by production code (checked by \texttt{grep}, not just asserted). Every one of
the 7 fixture cases also has a real, committed report in \path{eval/reports/*.json}, produced by
actually running the pipeline end to end, not hand-written (Table~\ref{ch8:tab:fixture-results}).

\subsubsection{Limitations and a failure case}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{No numeric confidence score.} Reliability is always matching failures out of $N$
    replays plus an interval, never a single number --- a deliberate choice, not a gap.
  \item \textbf{\texttt{BELOW\_CONFIDENCE\_THRESHOLD} is reserved, never emitted.} \texttt{CANDIDATE}
    is used instead for a reproducing-but-below-threshold sequence, a team decision recorded in
    the report-schema contract.
  \item \textbf{No replay command in the certificate.} The schema has no field that serialises
    \texttt{reduced\_sequence} into a runnable command string --- found while writing Chapter 4's
    requirements traceability table, a real gap against FR-6, not fixed yet.
  \item \textbf{The random-order baseline (claim B11) is only partially run.} Our own baseline
    ran for real on F1--F4; published comparators (iFixFlakies, iDFlakies) are not yet
    integrated.
  \item \textbf{31 shuffles is Member 2's assumption, not mine} --- reused here only because
    \texttt{decide()} consumes whatever \texttt{infrastructure\_failures} count it reports.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Failure case: N2's flakiness mechanism.} N2 is meant to fail at random, independent of
order, so that a diagnosis never blames a polluter for it. Its original mechanism read
\texttt{System.nanoTime()}'s lowest bit; on at least one real machine that bit was
deterministically 0, so N2 passed 100\% of the time there --- the opposite of the negative
control's purpose, and the same root cause Member 2's Chapter 6 section independently observed
from the runner side (N2 returning \texttt{NOT\_REPRODUCED} when it should have been
intermittent). I replaced the mechanism with \texttt{new Random().nextBoolean()}, which mixes
\texttt{nanoTime()} through a full linear congruential generator rather than exposing one raw
timer bit, and re-measured it for real on two platforms after the fix: 11/20 (55\%,
Windows/JDK24) and 10/20 (50\%, Linux/JDK8, Docker) --- genuinely balanced on both, confirming
the fix addressed the mechanism rather than moving the symptom to a different machine
(\path{docs/evidence-m3.md}). The committed report \path{eval/reports/n2.json} is a separate,
later run (9/20, 45\%) --- cited in Chapter 7's test-case table, not here, to avoid mixing two
different measurements under one number.
